source_text: Item quod adsignata oratione assidendi mos est quibusdam, non perspicio rationem, nisi quam pueri uolunt. quid enim, si Hermas ille, cuius scriptura fere \'pastor\' inscribitur, transacta oratione non super lectum assedisset, uerum aliud quid fecisset, id quoque ad obseruationem uindicaremus? utique non. simpliciter enim et nunc positum est, cum adorassem et assedissem super lectum, ad ordinem narrationis, non ad instar disciplinae. alioquin nusquam erit adorandum, nisi ubi fuerit lectus. immo contra scripturam fecerit, si quis in cathedra aut subsellio sederit. porro cum perinde faciant nationes adoratis sigillaribus suis residendo, uel propterea in nobis reprehendi meretur, quod apud idola celebratur. eo apponitur et inreuerentiae crimen, etiam ipsis nationibus, si quid saperent, intellegendum. si quidem inreuerens est assidere sub conspectu contraque conspectum eius quem cum maxime reuerearis ac uenereris, quanto magis sub conspectu dei uiui angelo adhuc orationis adstante factum istud inreligiosissimum est? nisi exprobramus deo, quod nos oratio fatigauerit.
thought_title: Sitting after prayer is not a rule
orientation: Tertullian is criticizing customs added to prayer, and here he rejects the practice of sitting down after finishing prayer as if it were required.
pass_a_gloss: Likewise, that after the assigned prayer the custom of sitting down belongs to some people, I do not see the reason, except the one which boys want. For what if that Hermas, whose writing is generally inscribed 'the Shepherd', after finishing prayer had not sat down on the bed, but had done something else, would we also claim that thing for observance? Surely not. For it is set down simply and now, 'when I had prayed and sat down on the bed', for the order of the narrative, not for the pattern of teaching. Otherwise there will be nowhere to pray, except where there has been a bed. On the contrary, he will have acted against Scripture, if anyone sits on a chair or a bench. Furthermore, since the nations do the same thing by sitting down after their little images have been worshipped, for this reason at least it deserves to be blamed in us, because it is practiced among idols. To this is added also the charge of irreverence, which even the nations themselves, if they had any sense, should understand. If indeed it is irreverent to sit down under the gaze and opposite the gaze of him whom you especially revere and venerate, how much more is that deed most irreligious under the gaze of the living God, with the angel of prayer still standing by? Unless we reproach God, because prayer has wearied us.

lemmas.gloss: we would claim, lay claim to

choices.why: Keeps the sense of a fixed, appointed prayer (the Lord's Prayer) that has been completed, matching the temporal force of the ablative absolute.

choices.english: I do not see the reason
choices.why: Perspicio means to see through or perceive clearly; 'I do not see the reason' preserves the skeptical, dismissive tone.
rejected: I do not understand the logic
I fail to perceive the rationale

choices.english: except the one which boys want
choices.why: Pueri here suggests childish, unserious reasoning; 'boys' keeps the dismissive edge without over-translating.

choices.term: ad ordinem narrationis, non ad instar disciplinae
choices.english: for the order of the narrative, not for the pattern of teaching
choices.why: Disciplina is a key glossary term rendered 'teaching'; instar means pattern or model, so the contrast between narrative sequence and normative teaching is preserved.
rejected: for the sake of the story's order, not as a model of discipline
for narrative sequence, not as an example of instruction

choices.english: by sitting down after their little images have been worshipped
choices.why: Sigillaribus is diminutive and contemptuous ('little images'); the gerund residendo is rendered as 'by sitting down' to keep the instrumental force.
rejected: by sitting after worshipping their idols
when they sit after adoring their statuettes

choices.english: with the angel of prayer still standing by
choices.why: Adstante is present participle 'standing by'; 'still' captures adhuc, and 'angel of prayer' keeps the genitive relation without over-interpreting.
rejected: while the angel of prayer is still present
with the prayer angel still attending

pass_b_english: I do not see the reason why some people have a custom of sitting down after the appointed prayer, except that they are following a childish whim. What if that Hermas, whose book is usually called “The Shepherd,” had not sat down on his bed after finishing prayer but had done something else? Would we claim that too as a rule? Certainly not. For even now it is stated simply, “When I had prayed and sat down on my bed,” for the order of the narrative, not as a pattern of teaching. Otherwise there will be no place to pray except where there is a bed. In fact, anyone who sits on a chair or a bench would be acting against Scripture.

Furthermore, since the nations do the same thing by sitting down after their little images have been worshipped, it deserves to be condemned in us for this reason too: that it is practiced before idols. To this is added the charge of irreverence, which even the nations themselves should understand, if they had any sense. For it is irreverent to sit down under the gaze and directly in the sight of someone whom you are at that very moment revering and venerating. How much more irreligious is it to do this under the gaze of the living God, with the angel of prayer still standing by? Unless we are reproaching God that prayer has wearied us.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker's argument by breaking the long passage into two paragraphs at the turn from the Hermas example to the charge of irreverence, and smoothed the final rhetorical question so the contrast between human reverence and the living God's presence reads naturally aloud.

notes.quote: except the one which boys want
notes.why: Unclear what 'boys want' refers to; possibly 'schoolboys' or a specific custom.
notes.fix: Investigate Latin; likely means 'the reason schoolboys give' or 'a childish reason'.

polish.changed: I clarified the rhetorical question about Hermas by breaking it into two sentences, so the reader can follow the conditional logic and the answer 'Certainly not' without losing the thread. I also kept the paragraph break where the argument shifts from the example of Hermas to the comparison with pagan practice.

notes.quote: Hermas, whose writing is usually titled "The Shepherd,"
notes.why: Reader unfamiliar with this early Christian text cannot place it.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening phrase so that the childish whim is clearly the reason for the custom, and smoothed the sentence flow while preserving every claim, qualification, and quotation.

notes.fix: Likely 'the whim of children' or 'childish caprice'.
